record.paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Larger empirical tests of the model
record.original_question: Repeat, on a much larger empirical scale and for additional balance or fringe-related indices, the paper's data comparisons between the critical beta-splitting model and real phylogenetic trees, including the empirical studies of splitting behavior and fringe distributions.

evidence.quote: Because our data studies of splitting and of the fringe distributions (Figure 9) were small-scale:
Open Problem 11 Repeat these data studies on a larger scale and for other indices.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the critical beta-splitting random tree model on n leaves, defined as follows. Starting from a root clade of size n, recursively split each clade of size m ≥ 2 into two sub-clades of sizes i and m − i (1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1) with probability

  q(m, i) = (1/Z_m) · 1/(i(m − i)),     Z_m = sum_{j=1}^{m-1} 1/(j(m − j)),

independently of all other splits, continuing until every clade has size 1. The resulting random binary rooted tree T_n has n leaves. From this model one can derive, as n → ∞, a limiting "fringe distribution" describing the law of the subtree rooted at the parent of a uniformly chosen leaf (and its iterates), as well as distributions of standard tree shape statistics (balance/imbalance indices such as Colless, Sackin, cherry counts, and other fringe-based or split-size functionals).

Carry out a large-scale empirical comparison between the critical beta-splitting model and large databases of real phylogenetic trees, addressing the following:

1. For a substantial corpus of empirical phylogenies (across many taxa and tree sizes), compute the empirical distribution of split sizes (the size of the smaller daughter clade as a function of parent clade size m) and compare with the law q(m, ·) of the critical beta-splitting model.

2. Compute empirical fringe-subtree frequencies (frequencies of small subtree shapes near random leaves) for these phylogenies and compare with the limiting fringe distribution of the critical beta-splitting model.

3. Extend the comparison to additional balance / shape / fringe-related indices beyond those already studied (e.g., Colless, Sackin, total cophenetic, cherry counts, generalized fringe statistics), and quantify the goodness-of-fit of the critical beta-splitting model relative to alternatives (such as the Yule–Harding model and the broader beta-splitting family with parameter β).

Provide statistically meaningful conclusions about for which indices, and on which scales of tree size, the critical beta-splitting model fits real phylogenetic data, and where systematic deviations occur.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is an empirical/data-analysis open problem posed alongside the critical beta-splitting random tree program. Subsequent theoretical work on the model (e.g., the exchangeable partition representation and fringe-tree paper from 2024, and the heights paper) develops the limiting fringe distribution and related theory, but no published large-scale empirical re-examination across many balance/fringe indices comparing the critical beta-splitting model with real phylogenetic databases appears to have been carried out. Status appears still open.

status_evidence.title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Lists open problems concerning the critical beta-splitting model, including extending small-scale empirical data comparisons of splitting and fringe distributions to a larger scale and additional indices.
status_evidence.claim: The empirical comparison is posed as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree III: The exchangeable partition representation and the fringe tree
status_evidence.snippet: Develops the theoretical fringe-tree and exchangeable partition representation of the critical beta-splitting model but does not undertake large-scale empirical phylogenetic comparison.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent work develops theory rather than large-scale empirical comparison.

status_evidence.title: A Beta-splitting model for evolutionary trees
status_evidence.snippet: Earlier empirical studies indicate the β = −1 (critical) beta-splitting model gives a reasonable fit to many empirical phylogenies, but full large-scale multi-index comparison remains incomplete.
status_evidence.claim: Existing empirical comparisons are limited in scope.
